title: The Modern Defense
description: A tactical Black setup based on a kingside fianchetto which can be played against ALL of White's openings. Played by current GM Hikaru Nakamura and future GM Levy Rozman.

1rbq1rk1/2p1ppbp/2Bp1np1/3P4/4PB2/8/PPP2.text:
Even though Black is down two pawns, there's plenty of compensation.

It's in the form of multiple hanging pawns, open lines, and a lead in development. 

Black should be doing just fine.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1npbp/p2p1np1/3Pp3/P3P3/2N1B.text:
Black can spice up counterplay in several ways.

These include ...c6 to fight for the center, or maneuvering the f6-knight to d7 and striking with ...f5.

Either way, we have to fight against White's pawn structure somehow.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1ppbp/p1np1np1/6P1/P2PP3/2N1.text:
White forces us to move our knight.

d7 is the only square that makes sense.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1ppbp/p1np1np1/8/P2PP3/2N1BP.text:
Nge2 protects d4.

Once we have activated most of our minor piece and White's central presence becomes annoying...

We can finally attack the center!

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/p1np1np1/3Pp3/P3P3/2N1B.text: White may prompt the knight to retreat.

r1bq1rk1/1ppn1pbp/p1np2p1/4p1P1/P2PP2P/2.text:
When we're attacked on a flank, we counter in the center!

If White pushes to d5, it's crucial to stay active and jump to d4 instead of d7.

That way, if White pushes h5, we have options open to play ...f5 or ...f6.

r1bq1rk1/2p1ppbp/2Bp1np1/3P4/4PB2/8/PPP2.text: Taking with the bishop makes the most sense, as White threatens the rook.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/6B1/PQ1PP3/8/1PP.text:
White doesn't have to take the pawn, but it's probably the critical line.

Threatening a pawn and developing a piece.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1npbp/3p2p1/3Pp3/4P3/2N1B3/P.text:
And we can begin to launch our kingside attack.

The move ...f5 is important to fight in the center and give our pieces some space.

After that, we'll develop behind the pawn.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/1B6/3PPB2/2N5/P.text:
White may play Bb5 straight away to pin the knight on c6, contributing to the attack of the pawn on d4.

We simply develop our knight and prepare to castle.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/3P4/4PB2/2N5/PP.text:
Attacking the knight with the pawn is one logical way to do it.

We can counterattack the bishop while placing a pawn in the center. 

If White takes the knight or takes en passant, we will be able to open our bishop.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/3PPB2/2N2N2/P.text:
Nf3 is a logical attempt to defend the pawn on d4. 

However, White has to be careful after the following move.

...Bg4 pins the knight which is protecting d4, and capturing is an immediate threat.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/3Pp3/4P3/2N1B3/P.text: Retreating the bishop is also very logical.

r1bqk2r/1pp1ppbp/p1np1np1/3P4/B3PB2/2N5/.text:
White may drop the bishop to keep the pin alive.

Breaking the pin.

r1bqk2r/2p1ppbp/2np1np1/1B1P4/4PB2/8/PPP.text:
White temporarily sacrifices a piece, but renews the pin/threat on the knight.

Castling forces White to take the knight this move, as now the pin is broken.

r1bqk2r/2p1ppbp/p1np1np1/1N1P4/B3PB2/8/P.text:
White may find this sacrifice if they're smart.

Capturing is the only logical move.

r1bqk2r/2pnppbp/p2p1np1/6B1/PQ1PP3/5P2/1.text:
Defends e4 solidly with a pawn.

But ...c5 threatens the queen and strikes in the center.

r1bqk2r/3nppbp/p2p1np1/2P3B1/PQ2P3/5P2/1.text: Taking is natural as moving the queen allows us to take on d4.

r1bqk2r/4ppbp/p2p1np1/2n3B1/PQ2P3/5P2/1P.text:
Black is up in development, and has sufficient compensation for the pawn.

We'll finish queenside development and take the b-file, after which we'll castle short.

r1bqk2r/ppp1ppbp/2np1np1/1B1P4/4PB2/2N5/.text:
This is something we need to think about, as d5 attacks the pinned knight. 

But there's a good way to counter this.

And that's attacking the bishop, so that dxc6 is less scary of a threat.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p2p2p1/1pp1P1B1/3P1P2/2.text:
We initiate contact in the center, as White's center is vulnerable.

If White plays accurately, they might keep a very small edge after a move like Be4.

If not, they are going to have to deal with the complicated central tension.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p2p2p1/1pp3B1/3PP3/2N2P.text:
Not only does Black strike in the center, but also the c-pawn may support a queenside assault!

The position is equal according to the computer, but things could get really dicey easily.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppbp/p2p2p1/1p2P1B1/3P1P2/2N.text: White may expand in the center while taking some key squares away.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppbp/p2p2p1/1p4B1/3PP3/2N2P2.text: Kb1 is very thematic in queenside castling situations to protect the king.

r2qk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p1Bp2p1/8/3PPB2/2N2P2/P.text: White takes on c6, which is very logical, as to provoke doubled pawns.

r2qk1nr/2p1ppbp/p1pp2p1/8/3PPB2/2N2P2/PP.text:
Black has sufficient counterplay with open lines for their pieces.

We'll activate the knight and complete castling, as well as place our rook on the b-file.

A smart pawn break at the right moment could be ...c5.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/1B6/3PPB2/2N2P2/.text:
Only move not to lose material.

We'll force the bishop to make a decision.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/1B6/3PPBb1/2N2N2.text:
White may try to defend d4 by pinning the knight on c6.

This still exploits d4, as the natural Qxf3 would hang a pawn due to ...Bxd4. 

White is forced to double their pawns on the kingside.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/3P4/4PBb1/2N2N2/.text:
We always have to consider what happens if White attacks the knight.

We'll jump the knight forward anyway to put pressure on the pinned knight on f3!

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/3P4/3nPBb1/2N2N2/.text:
White's only move to avoid doubled pawns.

We'll take the bishop pair.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/3P4/4PBb1/2N2N2/P.text:
Qxe2 makes the most sense. 

Black has several options from here, with a flexible position.

rn1qk1nr/1bp1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p4B1/3PP3/2N2P.text:
The move f3 protects the central pawn.

We develop our knight, which could support multiple pawn breaks.

rn1qk1nr/1bp1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p4B1/3PPP2/2NB.text:
White defends the center, so that 7... b4 does not win a pawn for Black.

One of the more natural developing moves is ...Nd7. 

We're not yet committing our kingside knight, as the bishop on g5 might be a target.

rnbq1rk1/1pp1ppbp/p2p1np1/8/P2PP1P1/2N1B.text:
White's intentions are clear.

We can continue developing towards the center.

...Nc6 eyes d4, and plans ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/1pp1ppbp/p2p1np1/8/P2PP3/2N1BP2.text:
White prepares the possibilities of castling long and/or going Bh6.

We develop towards the center.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/6B1/3PP3/2N5/PP.text:
White keeps castling options flexible.

We continue expanding on the queenside, as is our plan.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/6B1/3PPP2/2N5/P.text:
This is an awkward version of the Austrian Attack, except the bishop is already on g5.

We can continue our queenside expansion.

Our bishop is coming to b7.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/P2PP3/2N1B3/1.text:
White's idea is to stop b5.

However, White is indicating that they are not intending to castle queenside after a4.

Black develops a knight, targeting the center.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p4B1/3PP3/2N5/P.text:
Castling queenside is White's most aggressive strategy, as they can prepare a kingside pawn assault.

We develop our bishop to the long diagonal, with the intention of playing ...b4, and taking e4 if they allow it.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p4B1/3PPP2/2N2N.text:
White develops naturally.

We develop as well, eyeing a central pawn.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p4B1/P2PP3/2N5/.text:
White may try to break up our structure. 

However, a4 generally indicates that White won't castle queenside.

Our most natural response is to continue expanding, while attacking the knight.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/6B1/Pp1PP3/8/1PP.text:
Most reasonable retreat for White.

We don't need to worry about defending the b4-pawn, as White taking it will cost them some tempi in the future.

We can just continue developing instead.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/6B1/3PP3/2N5/PPP.text:
This is a move we might also see, possibly with the idea to pin the e-pawn, which could be a nuisance.

It's played 5% of the time.

We begin our plan to expand on the queenside, especially in case White castles over there.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
4.Be3 is played more than 30% of the time, as White protects d4 and the bishop is harder to attack. 

The main idea behind ...a6 is to prepare ...b5, which will gain space on the queenside and give the light-squared bishop an outlet on b7.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PPB2/2N5/PPP2.text:
This is a move you might see White play, but it's not accurate, as the bishop on f4 can be a target for ...e5 in the future.

It's played only 3% of the time.

...Nc6 attacks d4, and there are a few logical ways for White to defend.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
This is the main line by White, and one of the more aggressive schemes. 

White's idea may be to develop the dark-squared bishop, move the queen to d2, castle long, and launch a kingside attack.

For us, ...d6 is played so that our knight can hop to d7, and prepare an ...e5 or ...c5 break in the center at some point.

rnbqk2r/1pp1ppbp/p2p1np1/8/P2PP3/2N1B2P/.text:
This follows the game Goryachinka-Sadhwani 2020. 

6.h3 is also designed to stop ...Ng4.

Nothing wrong with castling!

rnbqk2r/1pp1ppbp/p2p1np1/8/P2PP3/2N1BP2/.text:
This is a common move to stop ...Ng4 while also preparing a g4-h4 assault as well.

We'll just castle. Nothing out of the ordinary.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White puts a second pawn in the center.

Our bishop will be nicely placed on g7 to attack the center from afar. 

Black does not have an immediate threat, so White has some flexibility in this position.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first study of the first chapter! This study will cover some of the mainline with 4. Be3, as well as 4.Bf4 and 4.Bg5 for White.

White moves their center pawn to e4, which is the most popular move at all levels. 

The Modern Defense starts with 1... g6. Black's idea is to put the Bishop on g7, and depending on how White develops, Black will combat in the center.

1rb1k1nr/3nppbp/pq1p2p1/2p5/P2PP3/Q1P1B3.text:
Black's piece coordination comes to life, and White is super behind in development.

After ...Qb6, we are putting pressure on the key weak points in White's position, such as b2 and d4.

Our bishop on g7 might come to life soon.

1rbqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/8/P2PP3/Q3B3/1PP.text:
White moves the queen away.

We'll strike in the center, once again trying to open the diagonal.

Since we've offered a pawn, we want to speed up our play.

1rbqk1nr/3nppbp/p2p2p1/2p5/P2PP3/Q1P1B3/.text: c3 is very solid to defend the d4-pawn and form a pawn chain.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/8/PQ1PP3/4B3/1PP.text:
We'll assume that White snacks on the pawn.

...Rb8 is a good move to get a tempo on the queen while taking the semi-open b-file.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p2p2p1/1pP5/4P3/2NBBN2/.text: Taking is logical, as the tension can be stressful.

r2qk1nr/1b2ppbp/p2p2p1/1pn5/4P3/2NBBN2/P.text:
Black has a very solid position, with straightforward piece placement.

We'll look to capture the bishop on d3 and finish our kingside development.

Our queen can join on c7.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2NBBN2/.text:
White connects their rooks, and is possibly ready to use the queen-bishop battery.

We'll strike in the center, helping our dark-squared bishop open.

r2qk2r/1bpnppbp/p2p1np1/1p6/3PP3/P1NBBN2.text:
Our development is nearly complete, and we're prepared for counterplay.

We'll castle and strike with ...c5 at the right moment.

Our rook can also join the party on c8 at some point.

rn1qk1nr/1bp1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2NBBN2.text:
White castles.

We'll develop our queenside knight, with the intention of ...c5.

It is one of the most important pawn breaks, after all.

rn1qk1nr/1bp1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/P1NBBN.text:
White does the same, preparing to castle.

We'll develop our queenside knight, possibly preparing ...c5.

rnbq1rk1/2p1ppbp/3p1np1/p7/P2PP3/2P1BP2/.text:
We'll castle, and play for ...c5 here.

The position is equal, but Black has a lot of potential and easy play ahead.

Some logical developing moves include ...Nd7 and ...Bb7, but you can hardly go wrong with development here.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B3/PP.text:
White continues with their aggressive development scheme, preparing O-O-O and Bh6 in the process.

Expect to see this move more than 55% of the time.

Continuing our queenside expansion.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1BN2/P.text:
Nf3 is a less-committal move by White, because f3-g4 is no longer in play. 

It's played 5% of the time.

We will continue to expand on the queenside, and see what White does.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/3p2p1/p7/P2PP3/2P1B3/3Q.text:
White captures back with the pawn.

We'll simply develop and prepare to castle, attacking the e4-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/3p2p1/p7/Pp1PP3/2P1B3/1.text:
White can try to chip away at the queenside.

We'll take as we can't effectively protect the pawn anymore.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2NBBN2/.text:
White nearly completes their development, and prepares to castle.

We'll continue developing our queenside.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/P1N1BN2.text:
a3 does not really scare us. All it does is stop b4.

We'll still develop the bishop to the long diagonal and prepare queenside counterplay.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/P2PP3/2N1B3/.text:
This is a common motif by White to try and break up the queenside structure. 

We will push forward and attack the knight.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/Pp1PP3/4B3/1PP.text:
Nd1 is also very logical, this time keeping the bishop open.

We'll go ahead and protect b4.

Maybe not objectively the most logical, but Qxb4 is a "threat".

We can leave the pawn hanging! 

Taking the pawn will be a headache for White, as the queen will easily be attacked.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
This is White's most common move.

We'll play ...a6 to support the b5-square. This study will focus on White allowing ...b5.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White activates the knight.

We'll play ...d6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

Let's develop our bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study of the first chapter! 

This study will look more into Be3, and the variations where White allows ...b5. Even more of these will be covered in the second chapter! 

White goes e4.

We'll reply with ...g6.

1rbqk2r/3nppbp/p2p1np1/2P5/PQ2P3/4BP2/1P.text:
We can hit the queen first, and then recapture the pawn with the knight.

Black is doing fine for being down a pawn.

r1bq1rk1/3nppbp/p2p1np1/8/P2BP3/5P2/1PPQ.text:
Black has several ideas, and should have an interesting game from here. 

White still hasn't castled their king, which could prove to be a problem.

We'll look to play ...e5 in the center and improve with the bishop on the diagonal and the rook on c8.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/3p2p1/p2N4/Pp1PP3/4BP2/.text: White castles long, in lieu of their lack of development on the kingside.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/P2PP3/2N1BP2.text:
White may choose to break up the structure on the queenside.

We looked at that same move last chapter, but f3 was not played.

No problem. We'll just kick the knight.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/3N4/Pp1PP3/4BP2/.text:
The knight may look scary on d5, but there are no concrete threats besides the b4-pawn.

Which we will protect.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/8/Pp1PP3/4BP2/1P.text:
Nd1 indicates that White may not be all in on castling long.

As we have a lead in development, we don't mind giving up b4 to gain an initiative.

r1bqk2r/2pnppbp/p2p1np1/8/PQ1PP3/4BP2/1P.text:
White will likely take the pawn.

And we play a move we wanted to play anyway, with tempo on the queen!

r1bqk2r/3nppbp/p2p1np1/2P5/PQ2P3/4BP2/1P.text: White may decide to get greedy.

r1bqk2r/3nppbp/p2p1np1/2p5/P2PP3/4BP2/1P.text:
Retreating is very logical, as White may want to avoid risks.

Black clarifies things in the center.

r1bqk2r/3nppbp/p2p1np1/8/P2BP3/5P2/1PPQ2.text: White recaptures with the bishop which makes sense.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppbp/3p2p1/p2N4/Pp1PP3/4BP2/.text:
We'll play ...Bb7.

We have several ideas, and now that White has castled, we know where to attack!

We can capture the knight on d5, finish kingside development, and eventually push with the c-pawn and strike on the queenside.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B3/PP.text:
White makes a battery with the bishop and the queen.

We'll continue with our queenside expansion strategy.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2N1BP2/.text:
6.f3 delays White's commitment to how they want to approach the position and which side they want to play on.

It's played 19% of the time.

Black is positioned for a queenside attack, and is ready for what White has to offer.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
White goes for the standard Be3.

We'll prepare ...b5.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White goes for Nc3.

We'll take some space with ...d6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

Let's fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first study of the second chapter! 

This chapter will focus more on the "Anti-Fianchetto" lines where White goes Be3-Qd2. 

This study will focus on lines where White omits aggressive h4-g4 ideas.

White goes e4. We'll play ...g6.

2rqk1nr/1b2ppb1/p2p2p1/1pn3Np/4P2P/2N1BP.text:
We'll capture with the knight to activate the piece while keeping the rook's c-file open.

White will probably go Nd5, after which we can play ...Nf6 or ...e6 to trade or kick the knight away.

Our queen can slide to the c-file.

2rqk1nr/1bpnppb1/p2p2p1/1p4Np/3PP2P/2N1B.text:
White castles long, making their intentions clear to attack on the kingside.

But we're ready to break on the queenside with ...c5!

2rqk1nr/1bpnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP1P1/2N1BP.text:
We'll play ...Rc8, and the ...c5 thrust is coming next.

Our counterplay in the center will be much quicker than White's attack.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppb1/p2p2p1/1p5p/3PP2P/2N1BP.text:
When playing ...h5, we did weaken the g5-square, and White may try to utilize it.

We're not really concerned, and we're going to continue with our queenside development scheme.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP1P1/2N1BP.text:
White may start with the g-pawn, and follow it up with h4-h5. 

This shouldn't warrant an immediate reaction, as the g-pawn does not have an immediate "threat".

We continue our queenside development.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP2P/2N1BP2.text:
White is preparing for a thematic "Yugoslav" attack with h4-g4-h5, with the idea to rip open the kingside.

We're going to make it difficult for White to attack by using our h-pawn to serve as a roadblock.

If g4 now, we can capture.

r1bqk1nr/2pnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2N1BP2/.text:
If White castles queenside before committing to a kingside pawn storm, we're not worried.

We continue our queenside development.

r2qk1n1/1bpn1pb1/p2p2p1/1p2p2r/3PP2P/2N1.text:
Black has good counterplay with very little weaknesses to show for it.

The position is equal, but White has to worry about a lot of things after ...e5.

There is tension in the center and the h4-pawn is under attack.

r2qk1n1/1bpnppb1/p2p2p1/1p5r/3PP2P/2N1BP.text: White keeps their development flexible and prepares to potentially reroute their knight.

r2qk1nr/1bpn1pb1/p2pp1p1/1p4Pp/3PP2P/2N1.text:
White also develops the knight.

We follow through.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppb1/p2p2p1/1p4Np/3PP2P/2N1B.text:
White hops on the g5-square.

We continue to prepare our queenside counterplay.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppb1/p2p2p1/1p4Pp/3PP2P/2N1B.text:
This closes up the position, which is what we want.

Now that White took away the f6-square from our knight, we should play ...e6 to develop the knight to e7.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppb1/p2p2p1/1p5P/3PP2P/2N1BP.text:
Taking is logical by White to provoke our rook out.

Taking with the rook makes by far the most sense. 

Now the h4-pawn might be a target.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppb1/p2p2p1/1p5p/3PP2P/2N1BP.text: We block them with our h-pawn, just like we see in the main variation with h4 immediately.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP1PP/2N1BP.text:
White now has both pawns ready for attack.

Now, we make White's attacking job more difficult. 

Either they allow us to take on g4, opening the h-file, they take and let our rook out, or ...g5 locks up the kingside, which favors us.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP2P/2N1BP2.text: If White barges with their h-pawn...

r2qk2r/1bpnnpb1/p2pp1p1/1p4Pp/3PP2P/2N1B.text: White places their knight on g3, possibly positioned for an f4-f5 break.

r2qk2r/1bpnnpb1/p3p1p1/1p1p2Pp/3PP2P/2N1.text:
We're going to be able to undermine White's position, as White has left some weaknesses.

Pushing the f-pawn might not be the smartest decision now by White.

We should consider ...Rc8 and castling.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B3/PP.text:
White improves the queen.

We'll expand on the queenside.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppb1/p2p3p/1p4pP/3PP3/2N1B3/.text:
But we lock the center up with ...g5.

Now it's going to be much harder for White to attack.

We'll continue standard development from here.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP2P/2N1B3/.text:
White may also go for h4 immediately, making their intentions of a kingside attack clear.

This move is played 7% of the time.

We'll play ...h6 with an idea in mind.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2N1BP2/.text:
White plays f3, solidifying the center and possibly preparing g4.

Whatever attack White goes for, we stay consistent with our queenside counterplay which consists of ...Nd7, ...Bb7, ...Rc8, and ...c5. 

The idea is to counteract O-O-O with a queenside launch of our own.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
The bishop comes out to e3, as per usual.

We'll push with ...a6, potentially preparing ...b5.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White activates the knight.

We'll push ...d6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

Let's get our bishop to g7.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study of chapter 2! 

We're going to analyze the more aggressive lines in this study, where White goes g4 and h4.

It can look scary to the untrained eye, but if you study this chapter, and pay attention to the details, you should be in good shape!

White plays e4, and we reply with ...g6.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/3PPP2/2N2N2/P.text:
While this is a very natural developing move, Nf3 actually plays right into our hands.

And it's played 73% of the time!

We'll pin the knight which defends d4, forcing White to react.

r2q1knr/ppp1ppbp/6p1/1B1P4/1n1P1P2/2N1BP.text:
No need to fear, ...Kf8 is totally fine! 

We will be able to recover d5 and hold a grip on the light squares. 

White cannot attack our king anymore, and we'll maneuver our kingside knight to f5 via h6.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/3N4/3PPP2/4BP2/PP.text:
Nxd5 looks good, as White captures a pawn without damaging their pawn structure. 

However, it's actually a mistake.

We kick the knight away, and now the d4-pawn is ours.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/3P4/3P1P2/2N1BP2/.text:
Taking with the pawn is the most forceful, as the c6-knight is attacked.

But we'll be able to recoup the pawn in this case.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/3p4/3PPP2/2N1BP2/.text:
White should just ignore d5, and continue with their development.

We're going to solidify d5, and develop normally.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/3pP3/3P1P2/2N1BP2.text: Advancing the pawn is another try by White to take some central space and restrict our bishop.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/8/3PpP2/2N1BP2/PP.text: This might be tempting to open up an attack on d4, although, it's a mistake.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/1B6/3PPPb1/2N2N2.text:
White might counterpin our knight on c6.

But we can still take on f3. White can't recapture with the queen because our bishop is still attacking the d4-pawn.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/3P4/4PPb1/2N2N2/.text:
White may move the pawn forward to attack the knight. 

The following response is pretty thematic in chapter 7, where White goes for d4-e4-c4 structure.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/3PPP2/2N1BP2/P.text:
White's pawn structure is slightly fractured.

This looks like a move you shouldn't play, as White has two ways to capture. 

However, both captures have consequences!

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/3PPPb1/2N1BN2/.text:
Be3 is the most "thematic" move in the position, not forcing anything, while defending d4 with a piece.

We're still going to take on f3, as gxf3 is forced.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/3P4/3nPPb1/2N2N2/.text: Exploiting the pin, so that capturing the knight on this turn is not possible.

r2qk1nr/ppp1ppbp/6p1/1B1P4/1n1P1P2/2N1BP.text: White may give us a check. It's tricky to block.

r2qk1nr/ppp2p1p/2n1p1p1/8/3bPP2/2N1BP2/P.text:
With the possible absence of White's dark squared Bishop, ...Qh4+ is suddenly very scary for White.

And we are already pressuring their dark-squared bishop which usually defends on f2.

r2qk1nr/ppp2pbp/2n1p1p1/3p4/3PPP2/2N1BP2.text: White completes their queenside development and castles.

r2qk2r/ppp1npbp/2n1p1p1/3p4/3PPP2/2N1BP2.text: We have a solid position, and can long term try to exploit the doubled pawns.

r2qk2r/ppp1ppbp/2n3pn/3pP3/3P1P2/2N1BP2/.text:
But ...Nh6 is thematic to hop into f5 next, exploiting the light-squared weaknesses just created.

This is not the best approach by White.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PPP2/2N5/PPP3.text:
The Austrian Attack is symbolized by White placing all three of their pawns in the center, grabbing as much space as possible. It's all about central control.

It's played 15% of the time on average on the amateur level.

The idea behind ...Nc6 is that we're immediately pressuring the d4-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
The knight comes out to c3.

It's time for us to play ...d6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White plays d4.

We'll complete the fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This chapter will cover the Austrian Attack, where White lunges three of their pawns (d, e, and f) forward.

Not only is it one of the more aggressive lines, but it gains a lot of space for White. 

This study will focus on the very natural, but inaccurate 5.Nf3, which can be exploited by a pin. 

White goes for e4. We play ...g6.

r1bq1rk1/p1p2pbp/1pnppnp1/8/3PPP2/2N1BN2.text:
We're still going to stay flexible, while controlling the light squares more.

Our bishop is coming to b7 and the knight will reroute to e7.

Eventually, we can look to strike in the center with a move like ...c5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/2np1np1/8/3PPP2/2N1BN2.text:
White follows suit.

We'll play ...e6 to keep our pawns flexible, as we might want to go for ...d5.

r1bqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p1Bp2p1/8/3PPP2/2N5/PP.text:
White takes on c6 to avoid losing anything.

We capture back.

r1bqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p1np2p1/8/B2PPP2/2N5/P.text:
Retreating seems logical to maintain the pin.

However, after ...b5 we'll be able to win our pawn.

r1bqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p1Pp2p1/8/4PP2/p1N5/PPP.text:
But we utilize our bishop's placement as White can't take on a3.

Long-term, we eliminate one of our doubled pawns and c6 can be a weakness.

Black is doing great and already has an advantage.

r1bqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p1np2p1/1p1P4/B3PP2/2N5.text:
Unless White finds d5.

Stockfish gives ...Na5 as the best move here, however, taking on a4 also has a cool idea to it.

We can allow the trade and take.

r1bqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p1pp2p1/8/3PPP2/2N2N2/P.text:
White at this point likely commits to developing and castling short.

We'll do the same.

r1bqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2Pp2p1/8/3nPP2/2N1B3/PP.text: En passant does not faze us.

r1bqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2np2p1/8/4PP2/2N1B3/PPP.text:
We recapture with the knight, and will continue our development in a standard manner.

The knight will come to f6 and we will castle short.

We've successfully removed one of White's most important pawns from the center.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/1B6/3PPP2/2N5/P.text:
Although played only 2% of the time, Bb5 is a logical try to pin our knight and defend the pawn that way.

We'll attack the bishop, prompting Bxc6.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/3P4/4PP2/2N5/PP.text:
White attacking the knight is something to consider, and it's played 6% of the time.

This attacks the knight but possibly overextends the structure and opens up our bishop.

We can generally meet d5 with ...Nd4, as the bishop nicely protects the knight.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/3PPP2/2N1B3/P.text:
Be3 is the best way for White to defend d4, and it's played 13% of the time here.

In the previous study, the knight was on f3, so we could play ...Bg4, continuing the pressure on d4. 

Here, we don't have such a luxury.

We're not going to go for anything extravagant. The point is to remain solid and wait for White to provoke weaknesses.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/3P4/3nPP2/2N1B3/.text:
White develops a piece while attacking the knight.

We can protect with a pawn, utilizing our ...c5 break defensively this time.

r1bqk2r/ppp1ppbp/2np1np1/8/3PPP2/2N1BN2/.text:
We should assume that White doesn't make mistakes, and chooses to develop and castle.

We'll do the same.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PPP2/2N5/PPP3.text:
The Austrian Attack.

White is aggressive with three pawns controlling the center.

Let's attack the d4-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
The knight is out.

We'll take away some squares from White.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Both pawns in the center.

We'll develop our bishop first.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study of our chapter on the Austrian Attack.

This study will focus on other 5th moves for White, so that you can be prepared for anything!

White goes for e4. Let's play the Modern.

lessons.title: White Moves The Light Squared Bishop

r1bq1rk1/1pp1npbp/p2p1np1/3Pp3/4P3/2N2N1.text:
We'll retreat to e7.

We have some thematic plans with ...Ne8, ...f5, and maybe ...c6-b5 to still chip away at the queenside.

Black is doing well.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1ppbp/p1np1np1/3P4/4P3/2N2N2.text:
White attacks the knight, so where do we go?

...Na7 is not as bas as it looks. 

We will still be able to play on the queenside, and the knight will come back to life.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1ppbp/p1np1np1/8/3PP3/2N2N1P.text:
If White just waits around, we can get our pawn break.

Part of the purpose of ...Nc6.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/p1np1np1/3Pp3/4P3/2N2N1.text: Our knight is prompted to move.

r1bq1rk1/n1p1ppbp/p2p1np1/1p1P4/4P3/2N2N.text:
Our queenside expansion continues, and our knight will be able to come to life in a number of ways. 

...Nc8-Nb6 is one way. 

Also, the knight does support ...c6 for now, enabling us to push and possibly recapture with it.

r2qk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p1np2p1/8/3PP1b1/2NBBN2.text:
But we continue pressuring the center, like we saw in the 150 Attack.

The d4-pawn is a huge target and we might be preparing ...e5 soon.

r2qk2r/1bpnnpb1/p2pp1pp/1p6/3PP2B/1BN2N2.text:
Black employs a Hippo-like formation, where White has a space advantage, but has to be confrontational in order to gain anything from the position.

We'll castle and then play for ...c5, supported by our rook which will come to c8.

rn1qk1nr/1bp2pbp/p2pp1p1/1p4B1/3PP3/1BN2.text:
White chooses to develop with tempo in this variation, which does not faze us.

We're fine blocking with the knight.

rn1qk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP1b1/2NB1N1.text:
While natural, this blunders a pawn!

We'll take the knight.

rn1qk2r/1bp1npb1/p2pp1pp/1p6/3PP2B/1BN2N.text: Retreating and maintaining the pin makes sense.

rn1qk2r/1bp1npbp/p2pp1p1/1p4B1/3PP3/1BN2.text:
White defends e4.

We can attack the bishop that moved to g5.

rnbq1rk1/1pp1ppbp/p2p1np1/8/3PP3/2N2N2/P.text:
White patiently puts their rook in the center.

We develop the knight normally, possibly preparing ...e5.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/2BPP3/2N2N2/P.text:
Chosen 21% of the time, this is a very classical approach by White, developing both knights followed by the bishop on c4.

However, Bc4 plays right into our hands.

We get to play ...b5, a move we wanted to play anyway, with tempo.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Developing the bishop to e2 makes more sense, as White can castle next move, and the bishop is not a target for attack.

Although it's only played 6% of the time.

We'll develop normally.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP3/2NB1N2/P.text:
This is objectively the least accurate of all the light squared Bishop moves, as now the bishop blocks the queen's protection of the d4-pawn. 

Also, the bishop on d3 is bad against our pawn structure on f7, g6 and h7. This move is played 15% of the time.

We can immediately try to exploit White's weakness!

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p1B4/3PP3/2N2N2.text: You might encounter this move, threatening the rook.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/1BN2N2/.text:
Makes sense for White to retreat the bishop while maintaining the diagonal pointing at f7.

With ...e6, we stay flexible with our structure, while blunting the bishop.

rnbqk1nr/2p2pbp/p2pp1p1/1p6/3PP3/1BN2N2/.text:
White castles to safety.

We'll develop our queenside normally.

Now ...b4 followed by taking on e4 is an idea.

rnbqk1nr/4ppbp/p1pp2p1/1p1B4/3PP3/2N2N2/.text:
No harm done.

Once White retreats, we will finish kingside development and castle.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White prefers to take this approach, controlling the center, and developing both knights 30% of the time.

We don't know where White is going to develop next, so it's important to stay flexible with our development and adapt accordingly.

We continue with the start of our queenside expansion.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White goes for Nc3.

We'll continue with ...d6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Two pawns on e4 and d4 by White.

Let's activate our bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this chapter, we will cover White going for the two central pawns followed by the two knights to f3 and c3.
 
It's a flexible setup with a lot of central presence. 

In this study, we will look at White developing the light-squared bishop immediately after the knights.

White plays e4, and we go ...g6.

r1bqk1nr/2pn1pbp/pp1pp1p1/6B1/P2PP3/2N2N.text:
Our queen is attacked.

No problem... we wanted to play Ne7 anyway!

r1bqk2r/2pnn1b1/pp1p2pp/3Ppp2/P1B1P3/2N1.text:
This is our plan! 

We want to continue the aggression with ...f4 and ...g5 and attack on the kingside.

This is why we closed the center in the first place. We have an extremely strong grip on the dark squares now.

r1bqk2r/2pnnpb1/pp1pp1pp/3P4/P1B1P3/2N1B.text:
White finally cracks in the center, and we have a nice plan from here.

Advancing our center pawn now that White has committed.

This does close our bishop for the moment, but you will see our plan soon.

r1bqk2r/2pnnpb1/pp1pp1pp/8/P2PP3/2N1BN2/.text:
White retreats.

Our Hippo is complete!

r1bqk2r/2pnnpbp/pp1pp1p1/6B1/P2PP3/2N2N2.text:
White prepares Bh6.

We won't let them!

r1bqk2r/2pnnpbp/pp1pp1p1/8/P1BPP3/2N1BN2.text:
White is trying to get Bh6 in, which would aid a potential attack.

Which we will easily stop.

Our bishop is too valuable to trade like this.

r2qk2r/1bp1npb1/pp1pp1pp/3nP3/P2P4/2N1BN.text:
Black's pieces start to come to life!

Our knights protect each other, and we have straightforward plans of attacking on the kingside now.

We want to push ...g5 and grab even more space!

r2qk2r/1bp1npb1/pp1ppnpp/4P3/P2P4/2N1BN2.text: White can attack, but leaves behind some weaknesses.

r2qk2r/1bpnnpb1/pp1pp1pp/8/P2PP3/2N1BN2/.text:
White centralizes.

This is a common motif in the Hippo, to prompt White to make a decision with the e-pawn.

rn1qk1nr/2p2pbp/pp1pp1p1/8/P2PP1b1/2NBBN.text:
And we'll likely continue with our Hippo setup.

The knights will jump to d7 and e7, and we'll castle.

In general, the Hippo is a bit more passive but an extremely solid setup that allows you to provoke a mistake from your opponent.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/P2PP3/2N2N2/1.text:
This is a very direct approach by White to prevent b5, although it's only played 5% of the time.

Since we can't play ...b5, we will go for ...b6 and implement a Hippo setup.

It's characterized by the pawns on the sixth rank, both bishops fianchettoed, and the knights on e7 and d7.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/pp1p2p1/8/P1BPP3/2N2N2/.text:
Bc4 is now more viable because ...b5 isn't an idea.

We continue with our Hippo setup, while restricting the bishop.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/pp1p2p1/8/P2PP3/2N2N2/1.text:
Just like we analyzed last study, a completely acceptable way to develop.

Our Hippo continues.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/pp1p2p1/8/P2PP3/2NB1N2/.text:
Sort of like in the previous study, Bd3 is not all that accurate, as d4 is more loose.

We'll attack the center, taking advantage of White's setup.

rnbqk1nr/2p2pbp/pp1pp1p1/8/P1BPP3/2N2N2/.text:
White castles.

We'll develop our knight to e7, Hippo style. 

We didn't want to commit to f6 yet.

rnbqk1nr/2p2pbp/pp1pp1p1/8/P2PP3/2N2N2/1.text:
White castles.

Where do our knights go?

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White plays the Two Knights approach.

We'll go for our standard ...a6 idea.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
Developing the queenside knight.

Let's play ...d6.

rnbqk2r/2p1npbp/pp1pp1p1/8/P1BPP3/2N1BN2.text:
White also makes natural developing moves.

Now we have both knights placed on the 7th rank, ready to support pawn breaks and pounce on weaknesses.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study of chapter 4! 

This study will focus on 5. a4 by White, which is a common move to stop our ...b5 advance.

White starts with e4. Let's respond with the Modern.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p2p2p1/1pP5/4P3/2NBBN2/.text: Capturing our pawn only favors us.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p2p2p1/1pp5/3PP3/2NBBN2.text:
White may just wait around.

We'll take in the center.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p2p2p1/1pp5/P2PP3/2NBBN.text: A thematic try by White to chip away at our structure.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p2p2p1/2p5/Pp1PP3/2NBBN.text:
But we'll kick the knight first.

Once White retreats, we'll quickly get the knight out and prepare castling.

To stabilize our queenside structure even more, our queen will join on c7. In general, our position is harmonious.

r2qk1nr/1b1nppbp/p5p1/1pp5/4P3/2NBBN2/PP.text:
Black has a nice position.

The pawn structure on the queenside is a big asset.

r2qk1nr/1bpnppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2NBBN2/.text:
Good centralizing move.

We'll strike in the center!

r2qk2r/1b1nppbp/p2p1np1/1p6/3NP3/2NBB3/P.text:
We'll just play chess from here.

We'll castle and bring the rook to c8.

Our knight on d7 is flexible to improve to either e5 or c5.

rn1qk1nr/1bp1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2NBBN2.text:
White castles.

Once again, note that we're going all in on the queenside before committing to our kingside development.

It's paramount to set up our ...c5 break as soon as possible, before White gets too much development and space.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p2p2p1/8/3PP3/2N1BN2/P.text:
White chooses 5.Be3 almost 30% of the time, making it the most popular move here.

This is very similar conceptually to a 150-Attack, but there are no f3-g4 ideas, so it's less dangerous.

We should continue with our usual queenside expansion.

rnbqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p2p2p1/1p6/3PP3/2NBBN2/.text:
White develops normally.

As do we... on the queenside.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Both knights out now.

We'll play the standard ...a6.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
One knight is developed.

Let's go for ...d6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White places both pawns in the center.

We should fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
We are in the final study of Chapter 4.

The last two studies focused on an early light-squared bishop development. 

This study will focus on an early Be3, which is also thematic in a lot of Modern positions. 

White opens with e4, and we will reply with ...g6.

r1b1k2r/ppp1ppbp/2n3p1/4P3/2B3n1/5N2/PPP.text:
The pawn is attacked three times and only defended once. 

So we'll be up a pawn.

Best resistance for White is to play e6 and force us to damage our structure, but we'll be up a pawn.

r1bQ1rk1/ppp2pbp/2n2np1/4p3/2B1P3/5N1P/P.text:
White could decide to remove the queens off the board.

Either way, we play chess.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1npbp/3p1np1/3Pp3/2B1P3/5N1P.text:
We're in great position to play ...Nd7 and ...f5 for instance, and to steamroll White.

A move like ...c6 is always useful as well against the structure.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/2np1np1/8/2BPP3/5N1P/P.text:
This move stops ...Bg4 and possibly ...Ng4 if Be3.

But our thematic strike in the center is ...e5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/3Pp3/2B1P3/5N1P.text: White may lock things up and attack the knight, which favors us.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4P3/2B1P3/5N1P/.text:
This will force some exchanges, which is fine.

Recapturing with the pawn or the knight (allowing even more trades) is fine.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/3P4/2B1P3/5N2/P.text: Attacking the knight seems very natural.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP.text:
White castles, which is completely logical.

By playing ...Nf6, we prepare ...Bg4 since the bishop will be protected.

We also attack the e4-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp1ppbp/2np1np1/4P3/2BP4/5N2/PP.text:
This push does not really faze us. 

We'll have to trade queens, but it's a fine position for us as we'll win the e5-pawn.

We'll take the pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp1ppbp/2np1np1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP.text:
You might see this move, with the direct idea to defend the e4-pawn, and later try to counteract Black's ...e5 with Rd1.

But it allows ...Bg4 with no consequences.

White can defend on e4 using the rook.

We'll castle for now.

We're preparing our key move.

r1br2k1/ppp2pbp/2n2np1/4p3/2B1P3/5N1P/PP.text:
Black is doing totally fine with the open file, and lack of threats by White.

We are also slightly ahead in development.

r2q1r1k/pppn1pbp/2np2p1/4p3/2BPP3/2P1BQ1.text:
And after we move the king, ...f5 becomes a legal move and a crucial idea in our position.

If we manage to play it, we will possibly open up the f-file and reach key central control, with attacking potential on the kingside.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4P3/2B1P1b1/2P2N.text:
Capturing now runs into the same issues. 

Just don't play ...dxe5 and hang your queen!

r2q1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4p3/2BPP1b1/2P2N.text:
Prompting us to make a decision.

We'll take, removing one of the important central defenders.

There was no merit to retreating now.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4p3/2BPP3/2P2Q1P.text:
White captures back.

Now one of our most important ideas becomes the common ...f5 pawn break.

We'll maneuver the knight to d7 first, opening up the pawn and providing more support to e5.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4n3/2B1P1b1/2P2N2.text:
Same problems for White.

They will have to give something up.

r2qk2r/ppp1npbp/3p1np1/3Pp3/2B1P1b1/2P2N.text:
Our counterplay is just heating up!

We will go for the standard ...Nd7 and ...f5 idea, since that's our strongest pawn break.

We could consider capturing on f3 if we have a reason to.

r2qk2r/ppp1ppbp/2np1np1/8/2BPP1b1/2P2N2/.text:
White defends d4.

But we continue by striking in the center.

The move ...e5 is even more potent when the knight on f3 is pinned.

r2qk2r/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/3Pp3/2B1P1b1/2P2N.text: Once again, we're not really worried about White blocking up the center.

r2qk2r/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4P3/2B1P1b1/2P2N2.text: This is actually a significant mistake.

r2qk2r/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4p3/2BPP1b1/2P2N2.text:
Rd1 is a natural way to defend the d4-pawn.

We'll castle for now.

r2qk2r/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4n3/2B1P1b1/2P2N2/.text:
We're going to either shatter White's Kkngside structure, or grab the bishop.

Either way, White has allowed us too much activity.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/3P4/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
We don't mind retreating the knight back to its starting square.

White has committed to a lot with d5 and now there are some weaknesses in their position.

We'll continue with ...Nf6 and ...c6 to undermine the structure.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Nf3-Bc4 is a commonplace setup in chess, and it's played 17% of the time here. 

We shouldn't play ...Bg4 here because of sacrificial ideas on f7.

We're going to continue pressuring the center instead, with ...e5 in the future.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
White activates the kingside knight 34% of the time in this position, making it the most popular move.

With this setup, White usually wants to leave their options open for the c-pawn to move.

We'll respond with ...d6 anyway.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White places two pawns in the center.

We'll fianchetto our bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Chapter 5 will focus on White developing with Nf3, but not Nc3.

This study will focus on the combination between Nf3 and Bc4, and we will use ...e5 as one of the main central counterpushes in this study.

White opens with e4 and we will play the Modern.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1npbp/2n3p1/4p3/4P3/2NB1N1P/.text:
And we castle! 

White hasn't achieved anything out of the opening and has developed their pieces in a suboptimal way.

We'll continue with a comfortable game from here. If allowed, we can go ...Nb4, and if not, ...b6 and ...Bb7 seems fine.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/2n2np1/3pp3/3PP3/2PBBN1.text:
This is a nice move to throw in if the situation presents itself. 

Our center is well protected, so there's no worry in the world to go into this. 

If White captures on d5, we can capture on d4. If they capture on e5, we can play ...Nxe4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4p3/3PP3/2PBBN1.text: Same king safety procedures by White.

r1bqk1nr/1pp1ppbp/p1Bp2p1/8/3PP3/2P2N2/P.text:
On Ba4, we can play ...b5, a move we wanted to play, with tempo.

Instead, White captures.

r1bqk1nr/2p1ppbp/p1pp2p1/8/3PP3/2P2N2/PP.text:
This position is totally fine as we have the bishop pair.

We'll try to continue with standard developing moves.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1n1bp/3p2p1/3PpP2/2P5/3B1N2/.text: You may see this if White panics.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1n1bp/3p2p1/3Ppp2/2P1P3/2NB1.text:
White's best course of action is to develop normally. 

We'll continue to develop as well.

We don't want to take on e4 as that would only help activate White's pieces.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1n1bp/3p4/3Ppp2/2P5/3B1N2/PP.text:
Keeping our pawns in motion.

Now ...e4 is coming and White has allowed a lot of central space.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1npbp/3p2p1/3Pp3/2P1P3/3B1N2.text:
White may try to solidify their center and prepare queenside expansion.

But we will play on the kingside!

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/1B6/3PP3/2P2N2/.text:
This gives us no worry, although we have to act quickly since White wants d5.

We'll attack the bishop.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/3PP3/2PB1N2/P.text:
This is a natural looking way for White to develop.

But it allows ...e5, and we will gladly take advantage of that.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2n3p1/4p3/4P3/2NB1N2/PP.text:
White develops too. 

Prepare to castle kingside.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/3Pp3/4P3/2PB1N2/.text:
As we've seen throughout this course, we're happy if White closes the center.

The most logical retreating square is e7. Now ...f5 becomes the main idea.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/4P3/4P3/2PB1N2/P.text:
The exchange is fine... we can take either with the knight or pawn. 

Just not the bishop, because we don't need to give up the bishop pair.

We'll take with the knight here.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/4p3/3PP3/2PBBN2/.text:
If White waits around, we'll do the same.

Developing the knight and eyeing the g4-square.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/4p3/4P3/2PB4/PP3PPP.text:
And we can play thematic moves from here.

We'll get our knight to f6 and potentially h5 if we want to make room for the ...f5 break.

We'll castle short, naturally.

r1bqk2r/1pp1n1bp/3p1np1/p2Ppp2/1PP1P3/1Q.text:
Logical attempt to protect b4.

We'll take.

We want to split as many pawns as possible in White's structure.

r1bqk2r/2p1n1bp/1p1p1np1/3Ppp2/1QP1P3/2N.text:
With the queenside for all intents and purposes locked up, we can begin our kingside assault.

Very difficult practically for White to play.

They can't really advance on the queenside, while we have a direct approach on the opposite side of the board.

r1bqk2r/ppp1n1bp/3p1np1/3Ppp2/1PP1P3/2NB.text:
White attempts their queenside expansion.

We'll try to break up the structure.

r1bqk2r/ppp1npbp/2n3p1/4p3/4P3/2NB1N1P/P.text: Preventing your bishop from pinning the knight.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2P2N2/PP3.text:
This is a move you will see 9% of the time, the idea is to defend the center with their pawn.

White commits the pawn to the c3-square but wants a solid center.

We'll activate the knight, preparing ...e5.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/3B1N2/PPP.text:
Playing Bd3 first runs into ...e5, and it's played 8% of the time.

The move ...e5 is a pretty direct antidote to White's approach, as it closes down the bishop permanently and fights for the center.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4P3/4P3/3B1N2/PPP.text:
If White takes...

By all means, recapture and preserve your bishop.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/4p3/4P3/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
Castling.

We'll just develop and support e5.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Going for the Nf3 setup.

We'll play ...d6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White wants the center.

We'll fianchetto for now.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In Study 2, we continue analyzing positions after 3.Nf3 by White.

This study will focus on fourth move alternatives to 4.Bc4.

White begins with e4.

We'll reply with the Modern.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pnpbp/2n3p1/2p1p3/4P3/2NPB1P.text:
White attacks c5. 

Don't hang it!

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2np2p1/2p1p3/4P3/2NPB1P.text:
We defend c5, and will continue with our setup.

The knight will find itself on d4, and we'll make a light-squared battery with ...Be6 and ...Qd7.

r1bqk1nr/1p1p1pbp/p1n1p1p1/2p5/P1B1PP2/2.text:
But on c4 it might become a target!

We'll play ...e6 to restrict it for now and prepare ...Nge7.

At some point, ...d5 is a healthy idea in the center, grabbing some space with tempo on the bishop.

r1bqk1nr/1p1pppbp/p1n3p1/2p5/P1B1PP2/2N2.text: White develops the bishop to c4.

r1bqk1nr/1p1pppbp/p1n3p1/2p5/P3PP2/2N2NP.text:
White may rather go this way, so that the bishop is less of a target.

No worries, we'll continue placating to our structure.

r1bqk1nr/1p3pbp/p1npp1p1/2p5/P3PP2/2N2NP.text:
But Black has a perfectly playable position.

In this case, we'll activate the knight to e7 and castle, remaining flexible.

At some point, we can decide for the correct pawn push if needed.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1n1bp/3p2p1/3Ppp2/4P3/2N1B1P.text:
But we get our structure with ...f5, and can proceed normally from here.

We'll activate the kingside knight and castle.

We got what we wanted out of the opening.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/3PP3/2N1B1P1/.text:
Natural development by White.

We'll follow through, and strike in the center.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/3Pp3/4P3/2N1B1P1.text:
White locks it up, which we know by now is good for us!

We'll retreat to e7, and ...f5 becomes the priority.

r1bqk2r/pppnppbp/8/3P3Q/8/2N5/PPPP1PP1/R.text:
We can play chess from here, and we're not afraid to play ...Kf8 if we need to defend the bishop.

White's only active piece is the queen and they don't have enough attacking prospects to compensate for the sacrifice.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n2np1/8/2P4P/8/PP1P1PP.text:
Black will have good piece placement with ...Bg7 and ...Bf5, and be more than able to compensate for the pawn.

Plus, now White's pawns on the fourth rank are looking weird.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1p2p/5np1/5b2/4p3/2N5/PPPPQP.text:
But we protect again!

We are simply up a pawn and a central one at that, and will follow up with ...Nc6 and ...Qd7 and often long castle.

Eventually, we will play ...Bg7. White hasn't achieved anything.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pp1p/4q1p1/8/6b1/5NP1/PPPPQP.text:
Blocking makes the most sense.

We should just exchange and take away their castling rights.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3q4/6b1/5NP1/PPPP1P.text:
Bg2 sufficiently protects the knight.

And here's a theoretical move to remember: ...Qe6+!

We're either forcing Qe2, after which we trade and the king loses its castling rights, or Kf1, after which the same outcome happens.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/8/6b1/5NP1/PPPPKPBP.text:
Black's play is very straightforward from here.

We'll develop both knights to the natural squares and fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

Then, we'll castle queenside.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3q4/8/5NP1/PPPP1P1.text:
White blocks with the knight while developing normally.

But the knight is pinned multiple ways now!

rnbq1rk1/pp1pnpbp/6p1/2p1p3/4P3/2NP2P1/P.text:
White may adopt a similar light-squared strategy.

We'll follow through with our dark square dominance.

rnbq1rk1/ppppnpbp/6p1/4p3/4P3/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
So will White.

Once we've reached this position, we've successfully neutralized White's bishop on g2.

Now we can begin to focus on the dark squares, and get a strong clamp on the d4-square with ...c5.

rnbqk1nr/1p1pppbp/p5p1/2p5/P3PP2/2N2N2/1.text:
White develops the knight to f3.

And we'll develop ours behind the pawn.

rnbqk1nr/1pppppbp/p5p1/8/P3PP2/2N5/1PPP2.text:
White stops b5, though.

So we can transpose into a favorable Sicilian, controlling d4.

White is playing a Grand Prix setup now with the pawns on e4 and f4, and we already have the bishop on g7 which is a great antidote on the dark squares.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/2N3P1/PPP.text:
However, this doesn't transpose.

White wants to fianchetto the bishop.

We'll still aim for our center expansion with ...Nc6 and ...e5.

Their bishop on g2 will serve as a strong defender but nothing more.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/4p3/4P3/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
White develops the bishop to g2.

...Ne7 develops the knight while maintaining flexibility with our f-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
This looks familiar!

We play our standard move. 

If White plays any natural move (Nf3, Be3, Bc4, etc.), it will likely transpose to previous parts of the course.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/4P3/2N3P1/PPPP1P.text:
White might aspire to do the same.

We should control the center with a pawn, since White hasn't contested it in any way.

Sure, our bishop will be blocked for now, but so will White's.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/4PP2/2N5/PPPP2PP.text:
This is a reasonable try by White, to control the center in a unique way.

They want to preemptively stop our ...e5 ideas.

In this case, we will go for ...a6 and ...b5, driven by our previous lessons.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3P3P/8/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
We're not afraid of this move and the following idea by White, but we should mention it.

We'll take on h5.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/6p1/3P3R/8/2N5/PPPP1PP1.text:
White's idea is very often this exchange sacrifice on h5, but it doesn't work if we play our cards correctly.

We'll take, of course.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/8/3P3Q/8/2N5/PPPP1PP1/R.text: This might be good for White in hyperbullet, but practically, Black is up material, and White does not have many threats.

rnbqk2r/ppppnpbp/6p1/4p3/4P3/2N3P1/PPPPN.text:
White does the same.

We'll just castle.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3P4/2P4P/8/PP1P1P.text:
White can try to hold on to the pawn like a baby.

We don't mind gambiting the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3P4/7P/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
White develops naturally, giving up the pawn.

We don't have to rush with taking it, though. 

We can just fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p2p/6p1/8/4p3/2N5/PPPP1PP1/.text:
Going after the pawn.

We'll defend.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pp1p/6P1/8/4p3/8/PPPP1PP1/R.text:
White captures on g6.

We'll recapture with the f-pawn not to hang our rook in the corner.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3P4/7P/8/PPPP1PP1/.text:
Taking the pawn is very logical. 

We actually shouldn't recapture with the queen as after Nc3, we get a worse version of the Scandinavian.

We'll just develop and eye the pawn instead.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3P4/8/6P1/PPPP1P1P.text:
Taking is not forced, but logical.

We're suddenly exploiting g3, which opens the long diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3p3P/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.text:
This does not scare us.

We'll take a free pawn!

White is overestimating the power of their flank push.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/4P2P/8/PPPP1PP1/.text:
White plays h4 only 1% of the time, with the idea being to play h5 and break up the kingside structure. 

You can always play ...h5 yourself, but I have a different recommendation.

We strike in the center since White didn't commit there.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
One way that White can develop is Nc3 here, played 8% of the time.

White is delaying d4 and wants to protect the pawn first.

We will continue with our Modern setup either way

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/4P3/6P1/PPPP1P1P.text:
You might see people try to mimic your setup, although it happens extremely rarely. Give yourself a pat on the back!

We can immediately strike in the center, before White reinforces it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the sixth chapter  and our final one on 1. e4 by White. 

This chapter will focus on Move 2 sidelines by White.

As always, White opens with e4.

We will go for ...g6.

N1bk2nr/pp1p1pbp/2n3p1/8/2P1P3/4B3/P4PPP.text:
But we take theirs, and we'll be able to trap the knight in the meantime.

Black will emerge up material.

r1b1k1nr/ppNp1pbp/2n3p1/8/2P1P3/4B3/Pq3P.text:
White has to try Nxc7+.

...Kd8 makes the most sense for the king since it comes with tempo on the knight.

Even though it's in the center, White can't really attack it.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2pbp/2p2qp1/8/2P1P3/4B3/PP3P.text:
We'll open up the light-squared bishop and our pieces have scope all across the board.

The b2-pawn is still vulnerable and we have direct and easy developing plans.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1pbp/2N2qp1/8/2P1P3/4B3/PP3.text: Capturing the knight is the most logical move by White.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1pbp/2n2qp1/1N6/2P1P3/4B3/P.text:
White may go for a fork on c7. That will not scare us.

We take the pawn on b2 with our own attack on a1.

r1bQk2r/ppp3bp/2n2ppn/4p3/2P1P3/2N1BN2/P.text:
Makes sense for White to accept, as...

We can't castle anymore.

r1bk3r/ppp3bp/2n2ppn/4p3/2P1P3/2N1BN2/PP.text: And White castles long with check.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2P3p1/4p3/2PnP3/4BN2/P.text: Though dubious, you likely will face en passant should you allow it.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/6p1/2pPp3/2PnP3/3BBN2/.text: White may attempt to develop normally.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2p3p1/4p3/2PnP3/4BN2/PP3.text:
And our queen contributes to the defense/grip of d4.

White has given away their d5-pawn for no reason and now our position is much more open and comfortable.

We'll make sure to keep an eye on our knight on d4.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/3p2p1/2pPp3/2PnP3/3BBN2/.text:
But once again, our grip on the dark squares gives us good play.

Next, we can look to activate our knight to e7 and castle short.

After that, ...f5 could be an important pawn break.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2p1p/3p2p1/4b3/2P1P3/8/PPQ1B.text: White could put extra protection on their central pawns.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/3P4/2PpP3/3B4/PP3.text:
Black should be in good hands to fight a strategic battle centered on the dark squares.

We'll continue with ...Nf6, since our d4-pawn isn't under attack anymore, and castle short.

At some point, we'll play ...c5!

r1bqk1nr/ppp3bp/2np1pp1/4p3/2PPP3/2N1BN2.text:
White develops naturally.

How should we continue development now?

...Nh6 looks a bit odd at first glance, but we're going to reroute to f7 and continue our pursue of the dark squares (or ...Ng4 to harass the bishop if they allow it!)
