White places their bishop on g2.

And we'll go ...Bd7!

The devious idea is to go ...Qc8 and ...Bh3 and try to attack the kingside. 

There's not a whole lot White can do against our plan.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/3P4/2P1PP2/6P1/P.text:
White continues to push even more.

This might look good on the surface, since White is controlling a big portion of the board.

r1bqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/3PN3/2P5/6P1/PP2.text:
White takes.

We capture back with the bishop.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3pp1p1/3P4/2P1PP2/6P1/P.text:
But in reality, we can easily chip away at the central structure, and Black has a very healthy position compared to White's.

Our bishop is standing strong on g7, and we'll continue to fight for the center with ...c6, and place our queen on the active b6-square at some point.

r1q1k1n1/ppp1ppb1/2np2p1/8/2PP3P/2N4b/PP.text: White shouldn't capture but if they do...

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppb1/2Pp2p1/8/2P5/2N2N1b/PP.text:
Now the bishop is gone.

Apart from that, White's shelter is completely exposed and we will easily be able to attack.

If anything, White capturing on b7 would give us the diagonal as well.

Black is much better, if not winning.

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppb1/2Pp2p1/8/2P5/2N2Npb/PP.text: White can try taking, but we have a devastating move.

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppb1/2np2p1/3P4/2P4p/2N2NPb.text:
White can try counterattacking in the center.

That's usually a good antidote against a flank attack, but here White might be too late.

We'll capture on g3 and sacrifice our knight!

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppb1/2np2p1/7p/2PP4/2N2NPb/.text:
White will play Nc3 at some point.

But ...h4 is coming whether White likes it or not. Not much can be done about it.

Black is ready to rip the king apart.

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppb1/2np2p1/8/2PP3N/2N3Pb/P.text:
It may seem like White can capture with the knight, but that's a game-ending blunder.

We'll sacrifice, of course!

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppb1/3p2p1/3Pn3/2P5/2N2NPb/.text:
We continue to play against White's weak King.

Trading off one more defender would be great, which is why we played ...Ne5.

We have the h-file and will just continue to improve from here.

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/5NPb/PP2.text:
White drops back, which is the purpose behind Re1.

We will not give up our pursuit on the kingside.

Let's try to push and attack!

r1q1k1nr/pppbppbp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/2N2NPP/P.text:
White can try to defend Bh3 by playing h3.

However, now White shouldn't castle, because it would drop a pawn!

r1q1k1nr/pppbppbp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2.text:
Here's an example line where we get ...Bh3 in.

Attempting to trade the bishop, and weaken White's King.

This is great because we sometimes have trouble activating our light-squared bishop anyway in these kinds of positions.

r1q1k2r/pppbppbp/2np1np1/8/2PP4/2N2NPP/P.text:
So Black can play with the advantage of White not being able to easily castle.

We'll castle ourselves and play ...a6 to take away the b5-square.

If White goes for e4 here, we should play ...e5.

r2qk1nr/pppbppbp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
White develops naturally.

We follow through with ...Qc8.

r2qk1nr/pppbppbp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
White can castle...

But that means they are essentially allowing ...Bh3, because now they can't play h3.

r3k1n1/ppp1ppb1/2np2p1/8/2PP2qP/2N4b/PP2.text:
There's checkmate in two.

White has no moves but to block, after which we will capture on g2.

Good game!

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
You might see this idea by White, to play g3-Bg2 and control the long diagonal. 

We'll continue to pressure the center.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPPP.text:
White takes a different approach than examined in the last chapter. 

White is showing less commitment by developing their knight to f3.

We'll play ...d6 to open the square for our knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
This study will explore positions that arise after White chooses to go for the famous Catalan Setup. 

In this setup, White fianchettoes on the kingside, usually after playing the pawns to d4 and c4. 

We'll be able to implement our Modern motifs here too! 

White opens with d4, and we'll play ...g6.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1npbp/2n3p1/p2pp3/4P3/2PP1NP.text: But ...a5 slows down White's queenside play.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1npbp/2n3p1/3pp3/4P3/2PP1NP1.text: White goes c3, possibly preparing a b4-advance.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1npbp/2np2p1/1B2P3/8/1P2PN2/.text:
We'll castle instead, as now their pawn is pinned, and we can recapture it on the next move!

White hasn't achieved any advantage playing like this.

If we know our lines, it's easy to equalize.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pb1/2n2n1p/6p1/2NPp3/4P1PN/.text:
The last move I want you to remember is ...g5.

Having already played ...h6, this move completely restricts White's knight from getting back into the game.

Although it does weaken the kingside a bit, we have a dark-squared bishop that's a great defender!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pb1/2n2npp/8/2NPp3/4P1PN/PP.text: White is basically forced to play e3 and block their own dark-squared bishop!

r1bq1rk1/pppn1pbp/3p2pn/4p3/3P4/4PN1P/PP.text:
White castles as well.

But we have a dynamic position to counter the London.

r1bq1rk1/pppn2bp/3p2pn/4pp2/2PP4/4PN1P/P.text:
White takes some more central space on the other side.

But maybe they misunderstood our intentions after ...f5.

r1bq1rk1/pppn2bp/3p3n/4ppp1/2PP4/4PN1P/P.text:
We can continue to attack!

We are aiming for ...g4 next, with our knight also supporting that square.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pbp/n4np1/8/3Np3/1QP3P1/PP.text:
And so do we. 

We have an amazing center and healthy piece development.

We'll play ...d5 next and leave our bishop active against White's passive one.

Then, we can develop flexibly.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2n3p1/3pp3/8/3P1NP1/PPP.text:
White prepares e4, which is their main idea.

We'll develop our knight to e7, keeping ...f5 as an option, which is our main idea!

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2n3p1/4p3/4P3/5NP1/PPPP.text: White castles, and could use the semi-open file to their advantage.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/4p3/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text:
We'll protect the center further, which is to be expected too!

Our position is stable and our center is safe.

We'll finish kingside development next and castle.

r1bqk1nr/pppn1pbp/3p2p1/4p3/3P4/4PN1P/PP.text:
White retreats it.

We're going to develop our knight to h6 to keep the bishop open and prepare the possibility of ...f5.

As you already know, this pawn push is extremely helpful in some Modern positions.

r1bqk1nr/pppnppbp/3p2p1/8/3P1B2/4PN1P/PP.text:
White gives the bishop a safe haven.

We'll attack it anyway.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1pbp/2n3p1/1B2p3/5P2/1P2P3/.text:
Now our e-pawn is pinned, so f4 is a very interesting to try and exploit it.

We have to be prepared for these tricky lines White can throw our way.

The best course of action is supporting our knight which is defending the center.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1pbp/2n3p1/4p3/5P2/1P2PN2/P.text: White pressures the center further, which is to be expected.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1pbp/n5p1/4p3/8/1QP2NP1/PP1.text:
If they develop...

We can harass them.

This opens up our bishop again and forces their knight to move.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1pbp/n5p1/8/3Np3/1QP3P1/PP1.text:
White jumps to the center.

We've succesfully cut off White's bishop, but now we have to protect our central pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp1npbp/2n3p1/3pp3/4P3/3P1NP1/P.text:
White strikes in the center.

But we have enough defenders on the d5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp1npbp/2n3p1/4p3/4P3/5NP1/PPPP.text:
We develop our knight to e7 with the future possibility of playing ...f5.

This would give us further space in the center and on the kingside.

We'll castle soon as well.

r1bqk2r/ppp1npbp/2np2p1/1B2P3/8/1P2PN2/P.text:
White may give in and capture on e5.

Recapturing now would actually allow them to take again since the knight on c6 is pinned.

r1bqk2r/ppp2pbp/2n3pn/4p3/3P4/3BPN2/PPP3.text:
And we will activate our knight to h6 with a solid position.

Our ideas after castling mainly consist of ...f5.

If we get this additional space, dynamics change and we could consider pushing further.

r1bqk2r/pppn1pbp/3p2pn/4p3/3P4/4PN1P/PPP.text:
White develops and prepares to castle.

We'll castle ourselves.

r1bqk2r/ppppnpbp/2n3p1/1B2p3/5P2/1P2PN2/.text:
White continues to pressure the center.

We'll continue to protect it.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2p1p/2n3p1/3p4/3P4/1P6/PBP2P.text:
And we'll establish a pawn in the center.

Our bishop is coming to g7 and White's will be the one staring at their own pawn.

After that, normal development will follow.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/1B2p3/8/1P2P3/PB.text:
Threatening to take the knight and to take on e5 is another option White can choose.

That's why ...Bg7 is logical to defend the pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/4p3/3P4/1P2P3/PB.text:
Confrontational, but it does not scare us.

We'll just exchange.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/4p3/5P2/1P2P3/PB.text:
Trying to exploit the pin.

We'll fianchetto and protect the center.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/8/1P2P3/PBPP1P.text:
White goes e3, possibly with the idea to go f4 and unleash the bishop.

This is the common idea in the Larsen; White plays against the e5-pawn.

Now that the diagonal is clogged up, we can go ...g6 and continue our Modern setup.

r1q1k1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/4PNPB/PP.text:
White takes it.

We'll take back and now our queen is active.

r1q1k1nr/pppbppbp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/4PNP1/PP.text:
White controls the center further.

We'll go ahead and play ...Bh3 now, forcing the exchange.

r3k1nr/ppp1ppb1/2np2pp/8/2PP3P/4PNPq/PP3.text:
And we will bring the queen back to h3 as well, where it's the strongest!

Of course, we can't attack without more pieces present.

Which is why we will finish development quickly and castle.

r3k1nr/ppp1ppbp/2np2p1/6N1/2PP4/4P1Pq/PP.text:
Expect to see it attacked immediately, though.

This is part of why White captured on h3 in the first place.

We'll drop back to d7.

r3k1nr/pppqppbp/2np2p1/6N1/2PP3P/4P1P1/P.text:
White attempts an attack of their own with h4, trying to play h5.

But it won't last for long.

We'll attack the knight.

rn1q1rk1/pp3p2/2p1bbpp/3P4/3Pp3/2N3P1/PP.text: Let's show the plans for both sides if White decides to trade in the center as well.

rn1q1rk1/pp3p2/4bbpp/3p4/3Pp3/2N3P1/PPN1.text:
From this position forward, White might want to undermine our structure with moves like f3.

Activating the knight to b4 and the queen to d2 are good developing moves.

On the other hand, we've almost finished development. We'll play ...Nc6, activate the queen and connect the rooks.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pb1/2p1bBpp/3p4/2PPp3/2N3P1/.text:
If they take...

We can simply recapture with the bishop.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/2p1bnp1/3p2B1/2PPp3/2N3P.text:
White could try to reactivate the knight to c2.

Now we ask the bishop a question.

rn1q1rk1/pp4bp/2ppbnp1/4pp2/2P1P3/2NPB1P.text:
And we'll continue to develop towards the center.

The move ...d5 is coming which will bring life to our pieces.

After that, we can develop the knight to c6 if White takes on d5 or to another square, dependent on how the position develops.

All in all, Black is doing well.

rn1qk1nr/pppbppbp/3p2p1/8/3P4/5NP1/PPP1P.text:
White castles.

We'll follow through. There's not much White can do about it.

And not many White players are prepared to trade their light-squared bishop early in the KIA.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2p2np1/3p2B1/2PPp3/2N3P1.text:
Don't be afraid of White pinning your knight.

It is sufficiently defended and you can always kick out the bishop with ...h6!

Activating the light-squared bishop with more defense in the center first.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp1np1/4pp2/2P1P3/2NPB1P.text: White develops logically, maybe keeping O-O-O as an option.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pb1/5npp/8/2NPp3/6PN/PP2PPB.text:
White spent a lot of moves developing, challenging the center and getting the pawn back.

We still have a lot of room to develop and expand, though.

I like the simple ...Nc6 here, attacking the d4-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4pp2/2P1P3/2NP2PP.text:
White makes a waiting move.

How should we continue here?

Well, we should go for full central control, and ...c6 prepares the ...d5 advancement in this case!

White has given us the freedom to do this.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3P1B2/4PN2/PPP.text:
White develops the knight.

We're going to prepare ...e5, which assaults the "London Bishop".

In many of these first move alternatives, changing our approach to the quick ...e5 is the way to go.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3P1P2/3BP3/PPP.text:
Even if White plays f4!

We don't want to allow them the central space here because it would be hard for us to develop.

In this setting, fighting in the center immediately is the way.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3P4/5NP1/PPP1P.text:
White develops to g2.

We have a sneaky idea, to go ...Bd7 and ...Qc8, followed by ...Bh3 to exchange their fianchetto Bishop.

We saw this idea in Chapter 10.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/5P2/5NP1/PPPPP.text:
White continues with their development.

We now get our critical pawn break in the center.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4P3/3P4/3BP3/PPP3.text:
White exchanges.

We'll take back with the d-pawn, keeping a pawn in the center.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4P3/8/5NP1/PPPPP1.text:
White exchanges.

We'll capture back with the pawn, maintaining control of the center

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4p3/2P5/2NP2P1/PP.text:
White does something similar.

And we continue with our plan.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/3p2N1/3Pp3/6P1/PPP1.text:
White shoves the knight forward, but without any targets for the moment.

Their main idea is to put c4 into motion.

Simply developing, ready to castle.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/3p4/3Pp3/6P1/PPP1PP.text:
One of the most common moves is retreating the knight all the way to the e1-square.

As we can see, this is already pretty passive for White!

Their main idea, however, is to expand with c4 and challenge the center.

Developing here is never wrong, preparing castling.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/3pp3/3P4/5NP1/PPP1P.text:
White could try and challenge the center with d4...

But ...e4 simply grabs more space and attacks the knight at the same time.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/3pp3/8/3P1NP1/PPP1P.text:
White castles.

We'll nurture our center.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/4p3/3P4/3BPN2/PPP3P.text:
White continues to develop, as taking on e5 would allow us to activate our bishop.

We'll develop as well and continue to support e5.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/6p1/4p3/4P3/5NP1/PPPP2B.text:
White now challenges the center with a pawn.

We'll develop our knight to control more central squares.

Once we've accomplished what we wanted in the center, normal development will ensue.

rnbqk1nr/ppp3bp/3p2p1/4pp2/2P1P3/2NP2P1/.text:
White challenges our pawn center with e4.

We don't really have to react to it, though, as our position is pretty solid.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP1P.text:
White develops the bishop to the long diagonal.

We're going to establish a pawn chain followed by ...f5 to control the center even more.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/4p3/8/1QP3P1/PP1PP.text:
Now White goes for Qb3.

The queen is pressuring the b7-pawn together with the bishop.

An interesting defense is ...Na6, threatening ...Nc5 if White captures.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/4p3/8/3P1NP1/PPP1P.text:
The most common continuation of White's KIA setup.

White wants to play e4.

We have two pawns in the center and our Modern setup!

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/4p3/8/5NP1/PPPPPPB.text:
White could also castle here and go for a different setup, aiming for d4.

This gives Black a lot of space and isn't played often at the highest level, but we should learn how to face it anyway.

Grabbing central space with the two pawns is always good.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
White often goes g3, with the idea to go Bg2, and control the d5-square in conjunction with their other pieces.

Since White hasn't immediately challenged the center, we'll take some space.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
White continue their London approach.

We'll play ...d6, though, and the position is much different than the traditional London where our pawn is on d5.

White's bishop isn't as strong.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3P4/3BP3/PPP2PPP.text:
White develops their bishop.

But now we will play ...d6, with the idea to go ...e5.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3P4/5NP1/PPP1PP1.text:
White may choose to take the center immediately.

This is more Reti style.

We'll continue to play in the style of the Modern. Our setup works against most of White's choices.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/5P2/5NP1/PPPPP2P.text:
This is a typical idea in the Bird's opening.

White connects the pawns on the kingside and wants to activate their bishop behind the chain.

Our idea is to go ...e5, though, and fight against White's structure!

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/8/2P3P1/PP1PPPBP.text:
So let's say White plays something else, like c3 to potentially build for d4 and restrict our bishop.

We'll gladly take the center here, anticipating White's move.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPPBP/.text:
White continues their similar setup to ours.

Honestly, if White goes this long without claiming the center, we should go ahead and do it ourselves.

rnbqk2r/pp3pbp/2p2np1/3p4/2PPp3/2N3P1/PP.text:
White continues with standard development, putting more pressure to the center.

Let's bring the king to safety.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pb1/5npp/3p4/2PPp3/6PN/PP2PP.text:
White is forced to retreat.

Capturing the knight with ...Bxh3 is a bad trade for us, as their knight isn't doing much!

And now simply capturing on c4 keeps the position comfortable for Black.

Playing ...c6 is also possible, but I recommend leaving the c6-square for the knight to develop to.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pb1/5npp/8/2pPp3/N5PN/PP2PPB.text:
White might go straight for the c4-pawn.

But we can let them take it!

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/5np1/3p2N1/2PPp3/6P1/PP2.text:
Challenging the center.

We want to kick the knight out first, before dealing with the c-pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/5np1/3p4/2PPp3/6P1/PP2PP.text:
The most logical continuation.

In this line, I recommend strengthening the center with ...c6.

We'll castle, develop the light-squared bishop, and then activate the queenside knight either to d7 or c6 if White trades in the center.

rnbqk2r/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4pp2/2P1P3/2NP2P1/.text:
White develops and prepares to castle.

We will castle as well, and the rook could be useful on the semi-open file.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/8/1P6/PBPPPPPP/R.text:
White follows through, attacking our pawn.

We'll go ...Nc6 to defend it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
White develops with Nc3.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
Of course, the London setups could be something you face even against 1...g6.

We'll continue developing for now.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP/.text:
White could play in the form of some stonewall with an early f4. 

The idea is to gain space in the center. 

But because of our setup, we're well-equipped to face it!

Nothing changes yet, as we continue our development.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/5P2/5N2/PPPPP1PP.text:
White develops normally behind the pawn, with more control over the center.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPP1P/.text:
White employs what's called the "King's Indian Attack", preparing Bg2.

It's like the KID, but on the White side!

We'll fianchetto, naturally.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/8/6P1/PPPPPPBP/R.text:
White fianchettoes.

We'll do the same.

Now Nf3 and ...e5 transposes to the Reti.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
The focus in the last chapter will be essentially all viable openings where White does not employ e4/d4, or d4/c4. 

While not the most traditional, these are useful lines to know.

White goes for 1.c4.

We'll respond with ...g6 here.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
1.d4 is technically not a move 1 deviation, but there could be move 2 deviations.

We will play 1... g6 as we normally do.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/5P2/8/PPPPP1PP/RNB.text:
The Bird's opening might look a little bit ridiculous, but it is extremely viable, and has been played by strong players.

It's simply an alternative way to control the e5-square.

We'll play ...g6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/1P6/P1PPPPPP/RNB.text:
White could try 1.b3, with the idea of Bb2.

They want to give up the center temporarily and then fight for it later.

This is a rare instance where we won't play ...g6 immediately, as it can get uncomfortable with White's bishop challenging the diagonal.
